summary: A 1976 paper about the design of distributed services, focusing on how programs at different network sites interact. It builds a model of those interactions and picks features that make services more reliable and responsive.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 722 describes principles for programs that provide services across a network. It separates the machinery for exchanging requests and replies from the rules for each particular service.

questions: how do network services stay in sync
what is the request reply discipline
how should distributed services match replies to requests
how does rfc 722 separate services from protocol machinery
subtitle: Design principles for reliable interactions between programs providing a network service.

tldr.problem: Programs at different sites need to exchange data and coordinate without confusing replies, losing data meaning, or breaking when service implementations differ.
tldr.mechanism: The paper models service interactions as requests and replies and proposes a general mechanism that handles data representation, synchronization, and extension separately from service-specific operations.
tldr.outcome: It presents the design basis for an interaction protocol and identifies RRP as one possible protocol using that approach.

today: RFC 722 presents a design discussion and says it is meant to explain the basis for the RRP protocol described in a separate document. It does not specify a complete service protocol itself.

sections.title: A Request-Reply Model
sections.content:
The paper calls the programs that provide a service servers and the user of the service a customer. Two servers communicate over a channel during an encounter; one acts as requester and the other as responder for an exchange.

The responder replies to each request. The requester interprets the reply as success, failure, or partial failure and takes the next action.
sections.plainLanguage: One server sends a request and the other answers it. The requester uses the reply to decide what to do next.

sections.title: Qualities of an Interaction Mechanism
sections.content:
The paper identifies needs for precise transfer of data meaning, separate handling of communication synchronization, support for service evolution, and reliable interaction among server implementations with different capabilities.

It also argues that a new capability should not require every existing server to change, while still allowing willing partners to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs need to understand the data, match replies to requests, and work together as services change. A new feature should not force every server to adopt it.

sections.title: Separating Shared Machinery from Services
sections.content:
The proposed architecture separates service-specific conventions from the general interaction protocol. The shared mechanism provides control requests and replies; each service defines its own user requests and replies on top.

Requests and replies carry sequence information so they can be matched. The paper says the mechanism should enumerate possible responses and provide a refusal for an unknown request type.
sections.plainLanguage: A common layer handles how requests and replies travel. Each service defines what its own requests mean, without rebuilding that shared machinery.
